question: Which S3 storage class offers the lowest storage cost for archive data that is accessed once or twice a year and can tolerate retrieval times of up to 12 hours (standard retrieval)?
option_a: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
option_b: S3 Standard
explanation: Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage class, with standard retrievals within 12 hours. Glacier Instant Retrieval offers millisecond access at a higher storage price.

question: Which EBS volume type generally gives better price-performance than gp2, with baseline performance that can be provisioned independently of volume size?
option_a: gp3
option_b: io1
explanation: gp3 provides a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s regardless of size, allows extra IOPS and throughput to be provisioned independently, and costs less per GB than gp2.

question: Which AWS tool analyzes resource utilization and recommends right-sizing for EC2 instances, EBS volumes, and Lambda functions?
option_a: AWS Compute Optimizer
option_b: AWS Artifact
explanation: Compute Optimizer uses utilization metrics and machine learning to recommend optimal resources, such as smaller instance types or different volume types.

question: A company stores log files in S3 Standard. Logs are queried frequently for 30 days, rarely for the next 90 days, and must be kept for 7 years for compliance but almost never read. What is the most cost-effective approach?
option_a: Create an S3 Lifecycle policy: transition to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 120 days, and expire after 7 years
option_b: Keep all logs in S3 Standard for 7 years
option_c: Move logs to EBS volumes after 30 days
option_d: Use S3 One Zone-IA for all logs from day one
explanation: Lifecycle transitions match storage class to access patterns: IA for occasional access, Deep Archive for long-term retention, and expiration when retention ends.

question: A company has a fault-tolerant, stateless batch processing workload that can be interrupted and resumed. Which compute purchasing option minimizes cost?
option_a: EC2 Spot Instances, ideally across multiple instance types and AZs
option_b: On-Demand Instances
explanation: Spot offers large discounts for interruptible workloads; diversifying across instance types and AZs improves the chance of getting and keeping capacity.

question: Instances in private subnets transfer large amounts of data to Amazon S3 through a NAT gateway, and NAT gateway data processing charges are high. How can a solutions architect reduce this cost?
option_a: Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint so S3 traffic bypasses the NAT gateway
option_b: Add a second NAT gateway
option_c: Move the instances to a different AZ
explanation: S3 gateway endpoints have no hourly or data processing charges, so routing S3 traffic through them removes NAT gateway per-GB fees for that traffic.

question: A company runs a steady baseline of EC2, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda usage and wants to reduce costs while keeping flexibility to change instance families and Regions. Which option is best?
option_a: Compute Savings Plans
option_b: EC2 Instance Savings Plans
option_c: Standard Reserved Instances for a specific instance type
explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2 regardless of family, size, OS, or Region, and also to Fargate and Lambda. EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Standard RIs are tied to a family or instance type in a Region.

question: A development environment runs on EC2 instances that are used only during business hours on weekdays. What is the simplest way to reduce cost?
option_a: Stop the instances outside business hours using a schedule (for example, EventBridge Scheduler with Systems Manager Automation)
option_b: Buy 3-year Reserved Instances for the instances
option_d: Increase the instance sizes so tasks finish faster
explanation: Stopping instances when not in use removes compute charges for roughly 70% of the week. Reserving capacity used only ~25% of the time wastes the commitment.

question: A company has an S3 bucket with data whose access patterns are unknown and change over time. It wants to optimize storage costs automatically without retrieval fees or operational overhead. Which storage class should it use?
option_a: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
option_b: S3 Standard-IA
explanation: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers based on access, with no retrieval fees, for a small per-object monitoring fee.

question: A company wants to reduce the cost of a new, infrequently used internal API with unpredictable traffic. Which TWO choices minimize cost when the API is idle? (Choose TWO.)
option_a: Implement the API with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda
option_b: Store data in Amazon DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode
option_c: Run two m5.4xlarge On-Demand instances behind an ALB
option_d: Use an RDS Multi-AZ provisioned instance sized for peak
option_e: Buy 3-year Reserved Instances for peak capacity
explanation: API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB on-demand all charge per request, so an idle API costs very little. Always-on instances and peak-sized databases cost the same whether or not they are used.

question: A company's Aurora MySQL database for an internal reporting tool is busy for a few hours a day and idle the rest of the time, but must respond immediately when users arrive. Which option reduces cost while meeting this requirement?
option_a: Aurora Serverless v2, which scales capacity in fine-grained increments based on load
option_b: A larger provisioned Aurora instance with Reserved Instances
explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity up and down quickly with demand, so you pay for what is used during busy hours and much less when idle. Self-managed MySQL on Spot risks interruptions.

question: A company transfers 50 TB per month from EC2 instances in one Region to users on the internet, mostly the same video files. Data transfer costs are high. What should a solutions architect recommend?
option_a: Serve the files through Amazon CloudFront, which reduces origin data transfer and often has lower per-GB pricing to the internet
option_b: Move the files to EBS volumes
option_c: Use a larger EC2 instance type
explanation: CloudFront caches repeated content at the edge, so the origin sends each file once per edge cache. Data transfer from AWS origins to CloudFront is free, and CloudFront delivery pricing is generally lower than direct internet egress.

question: A company runs a containerized web application on Amazon ECS with EC2 launch type. Cluster utilization averages 25% because tasks are spread across many large instances. Which change most directly reduces cost without changing the application?
option_a: Use ECS capacity providers with managed scaling and a binpack placement strategy, and right-size the instance types
option_b: Switch every task to the largest possible CPU and memory settings
option_d: Run each task on its own dedicated instance
explanation: Managed scaling with binpack placement packs tasks onto fewer instances and scales the cluster with demand; right-sizing removes waste. Alternatively, Fargate removes instance management altogether.

question: A company has many EBS snapshots from deleted instances, some over three years old, and old AMIs that nobody uses. Storage costs keep growing. What is the best long-term approach?
option_a: Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup policies to retain only required snapshots and AMIs, and archive older snapshots required for compliance to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier
option_b: Copy all snapshots to another Region
option_c: Convert the snapshots to io2 volumes
option_d: Keep all snapshots and buy Savings Plans
explanation: Lifecycle policies automate retention and deletion, and EBS Snapshots Archive lowers cost for snapshots that must be kept long term but are rarely restored. Savings Plans do not apply to storage.

question: A company's web tier runs on On-Demand EC2 instances. Baseline traffic needs 10 instances 24/7, and daily peaks need up to 30 instances for a few hours. Which TWO actions reduce cost while keeping availability? (Choose TWO.)
option_a: Cover the 10-instance baseline with Savings Plans or Reserved Instances
option_b: Use an Auto Scaling group that adds Spot and On-Demand instances for the peak using a mixed instances policy
option_d: Buy Reserved Instances for all 30 instances
option_e: Disable Auto Scaling and scale manually once a week
explanation: Committing only for the steady baseline maximizes discount without waste, and an Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy adds cheap Spot capacity (with On-Demand fallback) only during peaks.

question: A company's applications in three VPCs in the same Region all need to reach the internet. Each VPC has its own NAT gateways in each AZ, and NAT costs are high. Which design can reduce NAT gateway costs while keeping central control of egress?
option_a: Use AWS Transit Gateway to route internet-bound traffic from the VPCs to a centralized egress VPC with shared NAT gateways
option_b: Remove all NAT gateways and give every instance a public IP
option_c: Create VPC peering between all VPCs and use one NAT gateway in one VPC
option_d: Use S3 gateway endpoints for all internet traffic
explanation: A centralized egress VPC behind Transit Gateway consolidates NAT gateways, which reduces hourly charges as the number of VPCs grows (weighed against Transit Gateway processing fees). Peering is not transitive for NAT, and gateway endpoints only cover S3 and DynamoDB.

question: A company keeps 200 TB of rarely accessed files on premises that must remain accessible to on-premises applications through SMB, but it wants to stop buying storage hardware. Which solution is most cost-effective?
option_a: AWS Storage Gateway S3 File Gateway, storing files in S3 with lifecycle policies to cheaper classes and caching recently used data locally
option_b: Copy files to EBS volumes attached to a large EC2 instance
explanation: S3 File Gateway presents SMB/NFS shares on premises, stores data as S3 objects that can transition to cheaper storage classes, and keeps a local cache for low-latency access to recent data.

question: A data team runs a Redshift provisioned cluster that is busy only during a 2-hour nightly ETL window and for occasional ad hoc queries. The cluster runs 24/7. What change best reduces cost?
option_a: Move to Amazon Redshift Serverless, which charges for compute only when queries run
option_b: Increase the number of nodes
option_c: Buy a 3-year reserved node for the current cluster
explanation: Redshift Serverless automatically provisions and scales compute and bills only for compute used while queries run, suiting intermittent workloads. Reserved nodes discount a cluster that is idle most of the day.

question: A company runs a monolithic application on 20 always-on m5.2xlarge On-Demand instances. Analysis shows: average CPU is 15%; nightly report jobs take 3 hours and can be retried; image resizing triggered by uploads runs for a few seconds per image; and traffic during business hours is about four times the night-time level. The company wants the largest cost reduction with reasonable effort. Which plan should a solutions architect recommend?
option_a: Right-size and run the web tier in an Auto Scaling group sized to demand with a Savings Plan for the baseline, run nightly reports on Spot Instances, and move image resizing to AWS Lambda triggered by S3 events
option_b: Buy 3-year Reserved Instances for all 20 instances
option_d: Upgrade to larger instances so jobs finish faster
explanation: Each workload gets the cheapest model that fits it: right-sizing and auto scaling remove idle capacity, a Savings Plan discounts the baseline, retryable batch jobs fit Spot, and short event-driven tasks fit Lambda's per-millisecond billing. Reserving the current oversized fleet locks in waste.
services: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling;Savings Plans;AWS Lambda

question: A company stores 2 PB of data in S3 Standard across many buckets. Access logs show that 60% of objects have not been read in 180 days, 25% are read monthly, and access to the rest is unpredictable. Many objects are under 128 KB. Compliance requires 5-year retention. Which TWO actions will reduce storage cost most effectively? (Choose TWO.)
option_a: Use S3 Storage Lens and storage class analysis to confirm access patterns, then create lifecycle rules to move cold data to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive
option_b: Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the data with unpredictable access
option_c: Move all objects, including small ones, to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately
option_d: Enable S3 Versioning with no lifecycle rule on noncurrent versions
option_e: Copy all data to a second Region for safety
explanation: Analyzing access patterns and transitioning cold data to archive classes captures most of the savings, and Intelligent-Tiering optimizes the unpredictable portion automatically. Moving small objects blindly to archive adds per-object overhead and retrieval costs; unmanaged versioning and extra copies increase cost.
